title: Follow the person's whole task
outcome: Map a patient's goal across the kiosk, staff, and appointment system.
context: Mira arrives for a clinic appointment. A kiosk greets her, and a receptionist manages the arrival queue.
teach: User experience describes what a person goes through while pursuing a goal. Mira's goal is to let the clinic know she has arrived and reach the right waiting area. The kiosk is one touchpoint in that experience. Her reminder message, the entrance signs, the receptionist, and the eventual call to the consultation room also shape it.

Begin a task map with four labels: person, goal, starting point, and successful end point. Then place each action in order. Mira reads her reminder, finds the entrance, identifies the check-in route, enters her appointment code, receives a status, and waits. Beside each action, record the information she needs and the system or person that receives it.

A handoff occurs when responsibility or information moves between people or systems. The kiosk sends an arrival request to the appointment service. The service sends a receipt. The staff queue then shows the arrival to reception. These events can happen at different times, so the map gives each one its own line.

A useful map ends at the person's outcome. Mira reaches a waiting area with a clear expectation about what happens next. The map also shows a route through reception when she needs help. This wider view helps a team find the point where the service needs attention.
keyDistinction: The interface interaction and the service outcome are two connected parts of Mira's task.
workedExample: The team first sketches one box labeled 'Check in.' They expand it into entering an appointment code, sending an arrival request, receiving a service receipt, updating the staff queue, and showing Mira where to wait. The expanded map reveals a useful question: when does Mira learn that the clinic has received her arrival? The team adds that moment to the map before discussing screen layout.
guidedQuestion: The kiosk sends Mira's request at 09:02. The service returns a receipt at 09:02:03, and the staff queue updates at 09:03. Which map best represents her task?

options.label: Map the kiosk request and show the next step as soon as Mira presses Check in.
options.feedback: This captures Mira's visible action. Add the receipt and staff update as separate events so the map shows what the clinic has received at each moment.

options.label: Map the request, service receipt, staff queue update, and Mira's waiting instruction as separate events.
options.feedback: This gives the team a complete starting map. It connects Mira's visible experience to the system and staff handoffs that support her goal.

options.label: Map the staff queue update as the start of the experience and follow Mira into the waiting room.
options.feedback: This captures an important operational step. Extend the map back to Mira's arrival and kiosk action so her goal stays visible throughout the journey.

evidenceShift: A clinic that confirms arrival through reception would place the staff conversation and its confirmation at the center of the map.
transferContext: Receptionists use a queue that refreshes roughly every 90 seconds. Mira may ask them about her status while the queue catches up.
transferTask: Extend the task map through the staff queue and Mira's next step. Mark the source of each status and one place where she may seek help.
evidencePacket: Fictional service detail: the appointment service issues a receipt after accepting an arrival request.
Fictional service detail: the reception queue can display that receipt up to 90 seconds later.
Fictional access detail: reception staff can look up an appointment code directly.
artifact: A one-page task map showing Mira, the kiosk, the service receipt, the staff queue, and the waiting instruction.
assessmentFocus: The map starts with Mira's goal, follows the information through each handoff, and ends with a clear next step for her.
assessmentCriteria: The person and goal appear at the start.
Each status has a named source.
The map includes a help route and a successful end point.

title: Make each action understandable
outcome: Connect an action cue, system state, and feedback in the check-in flow.
context: Mira enters her appointment code and sees a button labeled Check in. The next screen currently says Done.
teach: An interaction becomes understandable when a person can see an available action, predict its result, and recognize what happened. A button label helps Mira predict that pressing Check in will tell the clinic she has arrived. The message after pressing it should describe the service event that actually occurred.

A system state is the condition the service is currently in. For this task, useful states include ready for input, sending the request, receipt confirmed, and request delayed. Feedback makes the current state visible to Mira. A brief progress message can cover the sending interval; a receipt message can mark the accepted request.

People form a mental model from the words, controls, and responses they encounter. Mira may interpret Done as confirmation that staff can see her arrival. The team can check that interpretation by asking her what she expects to happen next and observing whether she seeks additional confirmation.

Design the message and the underlying state together. A receipt-backed message can say 'The clinic has received your check-in. Please wait near reception.' A delayed request can show its current status and a staff-help route. This pairing gives Mira a dependable explanation of her progress.
keyDistinction: A clear status message names the event the service has reached and gives the person a usable next step.
workedExample: The team traces the current flow. Pressing Check in starts a request; Done appears before the appointment service replies. They move the confirmation to the receipt event and add a sending state for the interval. They then show the revised flow to Mira and ask what she believes the clinic knows at each screen. Her explanation reveals whether the labels support an accurate mental model.
guidedQuestion: The service reply takes several seconds. Which sequence gives Mira the clearest account of progress?

options.label: Show Done immediately, then update the message if the service reports a delay.
options.feedback: This offers quick reassurance. A sending message would connect the first screen more closely to the request's current state and prepare Mira for either outcome.

options.label: Show a spinner until the staff queue refreshes, then show the waiting instruction.
options.feedback: This ties the final message to staff visibility. A named sending state and a receipt-backed confirmation can give Mira earlier, more specific progress information.

options.label: Show Sending check-in, then a receipt-backed confirmation with the waiting instruction.
options.feedback: This sequence makes the transition and accepted result visible. Include a delayed route so Mira also has a clear next step during a service interruption.

evidenceShift: A service that issues immediate receipts can make the sending state very brief while keeping the final message tied to receipt.
transferContext: The kiosk receives a receipt while the reception queue still shows an older view.
transferTask: Write the kiosk message for the receipt state and a short explanation a receptionist can use during the queue delay.
evidencePacket: Fictional system detail: the appointment service issues a receipt after accepting the request.
Fictional operations detail: the staff queue refreshes every 90 seconds.
Fictional observation: Mira asks reception whether her check-in went through after seeing Done.
artifact: An annotated sequence for ready, sending, received, and delayed states, with exact status language.
assessmentFocus: Each message corresponds to a named state, and Mira can identify what action belongs next.
assessmentCriteria: The action label predicts its result.
The receipt message follows the receipt event.
The delayed state provides a specific route to help.

title: Design a route more people can complete
outcome: Find barriers in a task and give patients equivalent ways to finish it.
context: The clinic lobby has bright windows, background announcements, a standing-height kiosk, and a staffed reception desk.
teach: Accessibility begins with the task a person needs to complete. A patient may read the kiosk in glare, operate it while seated, listen through background noise, use a screen reader, or ask for help in another language. Each condition changes how the same check-in flow works in practice.

Review a task through four questions: how does the person perceive the information, operate the controls, understand the response, and complete the next step? These questions reveal specific barriers. For example, a color-only status can obscure whether an arrival was received. Text alongside color carries the status across more situations.

An equivalent route reaches the same service outcome. Reception can complete check-in when the kiosk route becomes difficult, provided staff can access the appointment record and give the patient a clear confirmation. The route also needs to protect personal information in a shared lobby.

Access needs vary across people and settings. Test the kiosk and reception route with patients who use relevant assistive technologies and with people in the actual lobby. Record the barrier, the route used, and the result of the full check-in task.
keyDistinction: Accessibility describes successful task completion across different abilities, devices, and environments.
workedExample: The team observes a seated patient reaching for a high control while the screen reflects sunlight. They lower the interactive area, increase text clarity, and place a visible reception-help instruction at the start. They test whether the patient can enter the code, understand the receipt message, and reach the waiting area. The full task gives the team a stronger measure than a control inventory alone.
guidedQuestion: The kiosk shows a green light for receipt and plays an automatic spoken message in the busy lobby. Which revision gives patients the strongest starting route?

options.label: Add a large check symbol beside the green light and keep the spoken message.
options.feedback: The symbol adds a visual cue. A text status and an intentional audio control would give more patients a precise, private explanation of the result.

options.label: Show a text receipt and labeled visual cue, offer optional audio, and keep reception help visible.
options.feedback: This combines clear status with patient control and a human route. Test reach, reading conditions, audio privacy, and staff availability in the real lobby.

options.label: Guide every patient to reception for a spoken confirmation after kiosk entry.
options.feedback: A staff conversation can support many patients. Confirm that staff can see the receipt and that the added handoff works during busy periods.

evidenceShift: A lobby with private audio stations can support a richer spoken route while preserving the same check-in outcome.
transferContext: A patient who uses a wheelchair and a screen reader arrives during a busy morning session.
transferTask: Map two usable ways for this patient to confirm arrival. Include the controls, status message, staff action, and privacy consideration for each route.
evidencePacket: Fictional setting: the kiosk stands near a bright window and background announcements play in the lobby.
Fictional operations detail: reception can look up an appointment code and confirm arrival.
Fictional service detail: the appointment service issues a receipt when it accepts check-in.
artifact: A barrier-and-route map covering perception, operation, understanding, and completion.
assessmentFocus: The routes reach the same appointment outcome and give the patient a clear confirmation in the lobby setting.
assessmentCriteria: The map names a specific barrier at each relevant step.
Each route reaches a confirmed arrival.
Privacy and the real lobby conditions shape the proposed cues.

title: Earn trust through clear promises
outcome: Explain what the clinic asks, what it knows, and what happens next.
context: The kiosk asks Mira for her appointment code and surname before showing her appointment details.
teach: Trust grows when a service makes promises that match its behavior. Mira needs to know why the kiosk asks for information, how her arrival reaches the clinic, and which step follows. The clinic can answer these questions with concise copy tied to real system events.

Collecting information has a consequence. A shared kiosk may show a name or appointment time to people nearby. The design should ask for the smallest useful identification input, show sensitive details with care, and clear the screen after the task. A visible staff-help route lets Mira resolve a mismatch through a person with appropriate access.

The stakes of an action determine the amount of review it deserves. Entering an appointment code can use a simple correction path. Confirming the wrong appointment deserves a clearer review of date, time, and patient identity. The confirmation message should mark the accepted arrival and describe where Mira should wait.

Review trust at three moments: before Mira shares information, before she confirms the appointment, and after the service responds. At each moment, ask what Mira can see, what the system has established, and what control she has over the next action.
keyDistinction: Trustworthy copy is grounded in purpose, accurate service status, privacy, and a usable correction route.
workedExample: The current kiosk asks for an appointment code and surname under a heading that says 'Verify.' The team rewrites the introduction to explain that the details find Mira's appointment. Before submission, the kiosk shows the appointment time and a way to correct the entry. After a receipt arrives, it shows where to wait and clears the shared screen after a brief interval. Reception remains available for a mismatch.
guidedQuestion: The kiosk finds an appointment whose time differs from Mira's reminder. Which first response helps her make an informed choice?

options.label: Show the appointment time and let Mira confirm check-in immediately.
options.feedback: The time supports recognition. Add a clear correction or staff route so Mira can resolve the difference before committing to this appointment.

options.label: Show the reminder time, explain that the clinic record has a different time, and offer reception help.
options.feedback: This exposes the material difference and gives Mira a route to resolve it. Confirm that the kiosk can obtain both times reliably before using this treatment.

options.label: Send Mira directly to reception whenever the displayed time differs from the reminder.
options.feedback: A staff route can resolve the conflict. Showing the relevant times first can help Mira and staff understand the issue and prepare the conversation.

evidenceShift: A clinic with a reliable self-service rescheduling route can add that option beside reception help.
transferContext: A patient finishes check-in at a shared kiosk while another person waits behind them.
transferTask: Write the final confirmation and screen-clear sequence. Show the accepted service event, next step, and privacy treatment.
evidencePacket: Fictional service detail: a receipt means the clinic appointment service accepted the arrival.
Fictional setting: the kiosk is shared and stands beside the waiting line.
Fictional operations detail: reception can investigate appointment mismatches.
artifact: A three-moment trust review and an annotated confirmation screen.
assessmentFocus: The design explains purpose, displays a verified status, supports correction, and protects the shared screen.
assessmentCriteria: Each requested detail has a clear purpose.
The final claim follows the service receipt.
The sequence includes a correction and privacy route.
